query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding approximately 5 at.% Al to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will promote the in situ formation of a protective alumina (Al2O3) scale during high-temperature exposure in air, thereby improving its oxygen resistance without compromising its room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr that exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹ but has inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Minor alloying addition by substituting approximately 5 at.% of the base elements with Al using vacuum arc melting.
generation.conditions: The alloy will be fabricated via vacuum arc melting, then subjected to oxidation testing in air at 800 °C for 5 hours; subsequent mechanical tests will be performed at room temperature and at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale that forms on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The introduced Al serves as a reactive element that promotes rapid formation of a continuous and protective Al2O3 layer during high-temperature exposure. This layer acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, thereby reducing oxidation while the underlying microstructure remains largely unchanged, preserving the alloy's mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-doped alloy will show a significant reduction in oxidation (lower weight gain and thicker protective scale formation) compared with the untreated alloy, while maintaining similar room-temperature ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits inadequate oxygen resistance in air at high temperatures, leading to degradation despite acceptable mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to cast, equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloys exposed to air at temperatures around 800 °C for periods up to 5 hours with subsequent tensile testing at room temperature and 1000 °C (strain rates 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹). It may not apply if the processing route or exposure conditions deviate significantly.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of alumina scale formation, the precise thickness and adherence of the formed oxide layer, and any subtle changes in mechanical properties due to microstructural alterations are uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and (2) the same alloy with a 5 at.% Al addition using identical casting and processing routes. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, perform oxidation measurements (e.g., weight gain, oxide scale thickness and adherence via microscopy) and mechanical tests (tensile tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C with strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹).
measurements: Oxidation weight gain per unit area
Oxide scale thickness and morphology (via SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (i.e., similar or greater weight gain and less protective scale formation) compared to the untreated alloy, or if the Al addition results in a measurable degradation of room-temperature ductility or high-temperature yield strength, then the hypothesis is falsified.

They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ]. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. chosen.lever: minor alloying addition (≈5 at.% Al substitution)
chosen.technique: vacuum arc melting to produce an Al-doped variant of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr followed by high-temperature oxidation testing
chosen.conditions: Exposure to air at 800 °C for 5 h combined with tensile testing at room temperature and 1000 °C (strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹) to verify that the Al addition leads to protective alumina scale formation without degrading mechanical performance
chosen.why: Previous oxidation protection research on non-equiatomic alloys suggests that a controlled addition of an oxide-former like Al can inhibit oxygen ingress. Since equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has not been tested and shows inadequate oxygen resistance, this experiment directly fills that gap by applying a well-established composition-change intervention to promote a passivating alumina layer while ensuring that both room- and high-temperature mechanical properties remain intact.
